rv.q: As an actor, Jones is an extraordinary vessel, holding these many people inside her and letting them speak through her, one by one.
Max Wolf Friedlich should know, since he has started to specialize in plays built around ideas that grab you, and then start accelerating.
Jones calls the production a “work in progress written by a work in progress,” a line that neatly captures both its provisional quality and its considerable vitality.
Jones’s characters feel so real because she approaches them all with deep and sincere empathy.
Jones raises so many questions and delivers so many truths that the message becomes murky.

Before the show began, an usher outside the auditorium pointed to a display that included an optional card to fill out – “Name a movement, gathering, or moment that is beautiful about America” – and two wicker chairs with “America the Beautiful” cushions festooned with some of the responses that audience members had already written.
America, Who Hurt You? is both diverting and unsatisfying, a call to action that lacks the passion that this moment arguably requires.

Much of this sad but true U.S. history—accompanied by TED talk–style timeline graphics presenting years such as 1776, 1619, and 1492—likely will prove familiar to the adult demographic who attend productions at TFANA.

In a year when patriotism has turned into a fight to the death, Sarah Jones offers something sturdier: a dozen-plus characters, one therapeutic intervention, and a hand-on-heart finale that asks a room of strangers to pledge allegiance to one another.
If you are as yet unaware of the talents of this writer/actress/activist, you owe it to yourself to take a trip to Brooklyn and revel in her presence.

cn.t: Jones dazzles with her virtuosic multi-character performance exploring American trauma, though critics are mixed on whether the ambitious therapeutic approach to healing national divisions fully succeeds beyond the impressive solo artistry.
